Prevention: Plough fields 14 days before transplanting during the dry spell to expose the cutworm to the natural enemies and the heat of sun
Place sticks next to or in contact with stems of seedlings.
Sticks confuse the arriving larvae so that they rarely find the okra plants
Conserve natural enemies like, spiders, parasitic wasps, praying mantis, ants, and birds by minimizing insecticide use; do not spray when natural enemy numbers are high.
Delay transplanting until the stems are too wide for the cutworms to encircle and/or too hard for it to cut to prevent cutworm damage
Remove and burn crop debris before planting
Monitoring: Additional relevant crops: okra, cabbage, cauliflower, peppers, tomato, potato, maize and cotton
Check fields for cutworms before sowing or transplanting.
Monitor damage by counting damaged and freshly cut leaves, freshly cut young plants, and holes in leaves and in stems
Check on plants daily for green to dark-brown caterpillars at base of plant and underside of leaves, observe for whitening or chlorotic lesions on fresh leaves and dried leaves
Early in the morning flush larvae using a mixture of lemon scenting dish washing liquid at 2 tablespoons/2 gal of water
If 5-10 caterpillars per 10 plants are observed, initiate control measures
Direct Control: Use flashlight to hand pick caterpillars at night or very early morning before they return into the soil
Flood field for 3 days before sowing and transplanting to suffocate and kill cutworm caterpillars in the soil
Drench at seedling stage with crude neem extract to reduce infestation drastically.
Apply at 35 ml/L of water during morning hours
Mix equal quantities of sawdust, bran and molasses with enough water to make mixture sticky and spread around the base of the plants in the evenings
